are also willing to form mutual relationships with humans. one outstanding example is in laguna, brazil, where dolphins and fishers have teamed up to catch fish for over 130 years.
a 15-year study conducted by researchers used drones and underwater cameras to observe this unique partnership. when migrating mullets approach the shore in large groups, some dolphins drive them towards the coast, where fishers stand ready to catch them with their nets. the fishers watch the dolphins, looking for them to communicate that they will be making a "deep dive," which lasts about 15 seconds. fishers then cast their nets just as the dolphins drive the mullets towards the surface.
as a result, the fishers catch much more fish, and the dolphins get to eat mullets trying to escape from the net. amazingly, dolphins that engage in this fishing are more likely to live longer, by 13 percent. without this cooperation, dolphins may end up swimming to areas where there aren't many fish, and in doing so, get caught in illegal fishing nests.
the 130-year partnership between the dolphins and the fishers of laguna is more than just a way to catch fish. it's a win-win for both humans and animals, a reminder of how our interactions and relationships with the natural world can be mutually beneficial. this harmony has kept the tradition alive for generations, and it continues to inspire us today
